  • 深入剖析當前熱門持久型 AI 助理（如 Mats、G-Bot 與 Claude Code Projects）的運作本質，釐清各家底層邏輯的差異。
  • 透過相同的資料蒐集與郵件發送實測，直觀呈現「分身模式」、「同事團隊」與「專案導向」在效率與穩定度上的鮮明對比。

摘要

什麼才是真正的「持久性」？三種架構的本質差異

作者指出，近期 Dots、Mats 與 G-Bot 等持久型 AI 助理引發廣泛關注，它們與過往聊天機器人最大的不同在於具備持久性（Persistent），即使關閉電腦也能在雲端自主運作。為了解開這些工具看似雷同的困惑，作者深入檢視後台設定，發現其本質完全不同：Mats 與 Anthropic 推出的 Claude DoIt 屬於「分身」（Avatar），透過單一連續對話與雲端記憶代表使用者本人執行任務；G-Bot 則是一個「同事團隊」（Colleagues），由多個各司其職的 Bot 透過群組溝通與派工協作；而 Claude Code Projects 則是以「專案/任務」（Project）為核心，由協調者指派執行緒完成清單，完成後執行緒即銷毀，僅保留成果與專案記憶。

實測任務一：資料整理與跨代理協作的效率對決

為了驗證三種架構在實際操作中的表現，作者給予三者完全相同的指令：尋找三部比較持久型代理的公開影片並整理成核心文檔。實測結果顯示，代表「分身」的 Mats 表現最省心，單獨一氣呵成完成整合表格，並主動提示過期資訊與盲點；身為「同事團隊」的 G-Bot 則遭遇協作斷點，在機器人彼此交接過程中出現停滯，需要作者如同管理者般主動催促才繼續運作，整體耗時 18 分鐘且檔案下載受阻；而「專案導向」的 Claude Code Projects 表現最為迅速，將任務拆解為四步驟清單，即便遭遇 YouTube 訪問頻率限制亦能自動繞道處理，在 3 分鐘內便把成果完整存入專案庫。

實測任務二：關鍵決策與安全審批的權限邊界

作者進一步強調，挑選 AI 助理的核心標準在於「面對可能出錯的關鍵行動時，決策權由誰掌控」。在發送測試郵件的實驗中，Mats 展現了嚴謹的權限控管機制，在未經授權前不會擅自發信，並提供單次批准或長期信任收件者的彈性選擇，且關鍵支付或資金轉移一律強制要求人工確認；反觀 G-Bot 在信箱權限與身分切換上則受限較多，並在安全審核流程中出現異常反應。作者總結，追求省心獨立執行可選單一「分身」，仰賴明確背景任務產出可選「專案導向」，而多代理的「團隊模式」則需要使用者付出更多監督成本。

================================================

# 三个常驻助手，越看越像

Dots, Muss, and Gkbot—you've probably heard these three names recently. They belong to the same category: AI personal assistants. Unlike the chatbots of the past, they are persistent; they are always there. Even if you close the window or shut down your computer, they continue working for you in the cloud, coming back to you once they're finished. And that is where the problem lies. All three are personal assistants, all are persistent , and all are racing to handle your emails, search for information, and book services. After looking around,. they seem more and more alike, and I don't know which one to use. I had the same confusion myself, and then I saw CloudCodeProject, which made things even more chaotic. It shares many similarities with these others, so does it count as the fourth one? In this episode, I’ll use the same task and the same test email to check these services. Their differences are actually hidden in one question: what exactly is the thing that’s staying persistent? Hey, hello, and welcome back. I’ve looked through a bunch of comparison videos, and almost no one includes CloudCodeProject in their reviews. Some people even asked when. Anthropic would release one, and as of today, they really have released one called CloudDoIt. But before that, CloudCodeProject was actually already there. It’s just that if you only focus on whether they can work automatically, they do look more and more alike. But once you open their back-end settings, the difference in what is truly persistent becomes immediately clear. Let’s first look at the Mats that I’m already using. Open the system files in its database, and you will see a list of system documents. Files like agent.md,.

# 分身：Muse、dots 和 Claude Duet

memory.md, and user.md—this structure is identical to the open-source OpenCloud. When you open the user.md file, the first line says, "You are not a chatbot; you are becoming someone." That means you are not just a chatbot; you are becoming a specific person. Memory follows you as that person, and files can be viewed, edited, and downloaded directly. So, what stays persistent in Mats is an alter ego, and Open's Dots fall into this same. category. Each account gets one Dot, starting from your chat memory. When you close the window, it continues to run errands for you on its own cloud computer; what it keeps persistent is also an alter ego. And the CloudDoIt that Anthropic just released also belongs to this category. It has its own cloud computer, a built-in browser, and maintains just one continuous conversation with you, inheriting the memory and connected accounts you already have in the cloud. It can check your email, calendar, and other accounts every few hours, and it will only come to find you when something. comes up. Before sending messages, making payments, transferring money, deleting files, or other actions, it will display the intended action exactly as is for your approval. Buying stocks or transferring money between accounts, even if you approve, it won't do it. It’s currently only available via a waitlist in the US, so I can't use it yet. Therefore, it is excluded from the following tests. Now look at the trial version of G-Bot I’m using; opening its list shows not one assistant, but two named bots. One is called "Mao-Tao," and the other is called "AI Radar." They each remember.

# 同事：Grok Bot 的两个 bot

their own preferences and roles, and every bot has its own independent chat page. More intuitively, if you click into the AI Radar conversation, it explicitly states "Message Source: Mao-Tao" at the top. They have their own communication records between them and will pass tasks to each other. So, what lives in G-Bot is not just one person, but a team of colleagues. Next, let's switch to Claude Code Projects. I specifically created a new long-term project for demonstration and wrote only one sentence in the goal field.

# 项目：Claude Code Projects

Inside the project, who I talk to is the coordinator, but the one actually doing the work is the thread it dispatches. Once the task is finished, the thread ends and is discarded. However, the project's memory and the things created remain within the project. So, what Projects hosts is a goal, or perhaps a mission. Here, we have obtained three terms: Avatar, Colleagues, and Project. The initial confusion has a preliminary answer, but relying solely on these three words is. not enough to make a choice. What are the consequences of really handing a task over to these three types of persistent agents? To see this consequence clearly, I conducted the first comparative test. I sent the exact same instructions, not changing a single word, to M, G-Bot, and Claude Code Projects. The only variable was the three entities receiving the task. The task was only one sentence: " Prepare a research package for the next video, find three public videos comparing persistent agents.""Organize the core points into a document." Let me state one thing here: Claude (the.

# 实测一：同一个资料包任务

model) did not re-run this research package task this time. Because it and M belong to the same "Avatar" category, and in the previous episode, I already used the same prompt, without changing a word, to have M and DS create the same hand-drawn animation. In terms of their organizational method, they are both one-on-one; you tell it, and it runs it itself. So, for this "Avatar" group, we will look directly at M's performance. Over at M, I started a new side project and sent the request over. I didn't need to nudge him once; he finished the work in one go and handed it back in an M document. Not only did. it clearly list the core points of the three videos and their reference value for this episode, but it also included a comprehensive comparison table. Even more useful was that it proactively flagged which information was outdated and added a specific note that all three videos found lacked in-depth testing of the Bot. Now, over at the bot side, the process was completely different. Every bot can actually chat individually, but its biggest feature is a group of bots working together. So this time, I specifically set up a group chat, pulled in Maotao and the. others, and gave them the same task. Maotao quickly replied, "I'll coordinate." Right there in the group, it tasked A-Radar to go find the videos . In about a minute, A-Radar found the three videos and posted them in the group. But after that, Maotao, who was in charge of coordination, didn't take over to finish the job, and the group just stalled there. After waiting a few minutes with no progress, I had to nudge them, telling them the videos were ready and asking for a summary document, only then did they go to summarize the subtitles. The whole.

process took about 18 minutes. In the end, they provided a readable text-based info pack in the group, but the PDF file sent to me privately showed "cannot read file" when opened in the app, no matter how many times I tried. Moving on to CloudCode Projects, I sent the same request in the demo project chat I had set up. The Coordinator immediately replied, " Understood, starting the compilation right away." It then automatically dispatched a specialized side, which listed out a four-step checklist and worked through it item by item. Midway. through, it hit a YouTube access rate limit, but it didn't stop to wait for me to intervene; instead, it noted the situation in the progress log, switched paths, and continued gathering data. In about three minutes, all four items were marked complete, and the finished document was saved directly into the project's library. You could open it and scroll through it. After running this same task, the results of these three tools were very telling. A single avatar is the most worry-free; you give an instruction and it handles it alone, but from start to finish, it's just one entity, whereas a group of colleagues will actually hand things off to each. other. But if the hand-off drops the ball, you have to follow up. You end up having to be the manager in the group chat. For a project, it breaks down tasks into threads, and in three minutes, it can place a document ready for reference into your files. But once the threads finish the job, they disappear on the spot; this file and this project aren't assistants that stay and chat with you, but they do handle research and documentation in the background. If you really want to choose an assistant to work for you,.

# 实测二：同一封测试邮件

what matters most is how it reacts when things could go wrong; for instance, when sending emails or changing things for you, who actually holds the decision-making power? This brings us back to the test email we mentioned earlier; it's the same test email, with the recipient being my own other inbox and the sender being an address I specified, with the only variable being which platform handles the sending. Let's first look at Notion; at the start, before I connected Gmail, it wouldn't send it directly but instead popped up a card to link the account. Once I linked Gmail and asked it to send again, it popped up an approval card: do you allow "Little Peach" to send this email? It clearly stated the sender, and below were three buttons: " Send,""Always allow this recipient," and "Don't send." So I clicked "Send." Only then was the email sent. You see, it defaults to leaving the decision to me, but if you trust a certain recipient, the card also gives you the option to trust them long-term. Furthermore, in the official design,. all of the agent's outgoing network traffic is governed by an independent sentinel. The agent only holds a proxy credential, and even payments require human approval for every single transaction; now let's look at GB. Its reaction was the most surprising. I asked it to send this email in the group chat, and it first told me the specified sender address couldn't be used. It could only use the bot's own email address. Then it proactively offered to draft a card for me to see; after the card popped up, I clicked the. "Send" button on it, but it replied that the security approval required for sending couldn't be completed in the group. Nothing was sent just now, and it asked me to talk to it in a private message instead. So I switched to the private chat window and sent a message to send the test email; in the private chat, it didn't pop up another card, the message went through, and the email was sent. At first glance, it seems like they didn't give you the approval rights, but that's not actually the case. I later had it send another one from scratch in a private chat, and it. still popped up a "Send" card, waiting for me to click confirm. The official documentation actually makes it very clear: when using the built-in email feature of GB, every single message requires you to manually click to approve. Having it send messages in a group chat doesn't count, and the approval card doesn't appear in group chats anyway; I only clicked it in the group. I had already clicked it; it can't process the approval in the group , so it asks me to go to a private chat to send this already-approved message. The rule for GlockB is that approval.

can only be given by you personally in a private chat. Also, you need to know that all bots under your account actually share the same persistent cloud computer; the official FAQ even states not to treat separate bots as security boundaries. With Open's D, I asked it to send this test email using a specific sender, and it replied, "Let me confirm if I can send from this address," and then immediately replied, "Sent and verified," sending the email without any approval or confirmation. process at all. If you don't want it to act so directly, you have to go into its "custom rules" to pre-set what is allowed, forbidden, or requires approval, as per the official instructions. Operations involving account settings or sharing information will undergo automatic review, and approval once doesn't mean long-term authorization. Since CloudCodeProjects didn't need to send external mail for the previous data packet task, no approval card appeared this time. By design, the thread runs in automatic. mode by default. Once it encounters an operation requiring approval, it will stop in that thread and wait for you. If a code repository is connected, it will also be constrained by repository permission rules, and any changes made will be submitted as a PR for human approval. So, looking at this whole process, everything boils down to decision-making power: the bot either asks you before acting, or you determine the rules beforehand in the custom rules and "always allow" settings. The second point is that approval must be given by you personally in a private chat, and since. they share one cloud computer, they don't have separate security boundaries ; the project keeps approvals within specific threads. Keep the output in the repository. Now, let’s look further into this—if it actually makes a mistake, can we roll it back? And when an error occurs, will you even be able to see it? If it's an email that has already been sent, all four are the same; none of them can pull it back. But if we compare the work they produce for the same task, it's a completely different story. The documents and code P produces, if committed to a Git repository, allow. you to revert to a previous version if something breaks. But if the corrupted PDF Gockbot sent me won't open, I have to ask it for another copy. When encountering problems, the visibility differs too. Projects inside will report YouTube stream issues in the logs and retry on its own, while during the minutes I spent waiting to nudge Glockbot, its screen just showed " Screen paused while you were away." OK, we've seen how they work. And how they.

# 四家怎么收费

handle quality control. Finally, let’s take a look at the bills and how these four charge, according to their official terms. For that, you need a P subscription, starting at $ 100 per month. It includes the first dot; chatting with D doesn't count against your quota, only tasks assigned to Codex or W are recorded. MILS has free and paid tiers at $ 20 and $ 100, distinguished by weekly quotas. As of October 12, GB merged into the unified X subscription, requiring at least the. $ 30 tier. The quota is shared with GCER in a weekly pool, and every reply in the group counts toward your usage. As for CloudCodeProjects, it isn't charged separately in P and Max, but the tokens they consume are deducted from the same quota pool, which will definitely be faster than single-turn chats, with a limit of 200 new Stripes per day. Additionally, CloudDoIt is free during the preview period and shares the same P/Max quota as other Cloud features, with background. searches and large tasks all counting toward usage. Alright, having said all that, the confusion from the start about which one to choose should now be easy to resolve. If you need help with daily chores and want someone to run errands for you, hand it off to your digital twin—choose M, or maybe D, or wait for the public release of Oud to see how Opic's Cloud performs. If you have several long-term business lines and want roles divided with mutual coordination, and you are willing to.

# 什么事交给哪一个

act as the manager in the group to push progress and oversee handoffs, then assign it to a team of colleagues— that is, choose GB. But if you have a specific goal at hand that requires delivery, acceptance, revisions, and the ability to roll back to a previous version, then entrust it to a project and choose CloudCodeProjects. So, back to the question at the beginning, does CloudCodeProjects count as the fourth one? It belongs to the same category, because it also stays persistent. It keeps working even after you close the window, but what it hosts isn't a. person. Nor is it a team. It's a goal; it wasn't competing with D in the same space to begin with. The one truly competing with D is Anthropic's "do it, " meaning Anthropic now has both. One for an alias, one for a project. Alright, so in our upcoming agent series, we will continue to discuss how to integrate these assistants into our daily workflows and what specific concepts they involve. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭開企業軟體交付與 AI 落地中「功能開發完成後，為何仍需工程師駐場」的核心挑戰與應對策略。
  • 深入解析 FDE（前線部署工程師） 的工作本質，說明如何挖掘未成文的「隱性知識」並調和多方業務歧異。
  • 提供清晰的「交付工作三層架構」，協助團隊有效區分核心通用模組、客製化配置以及業務邊界定義。

摘要

走進現場：為什麼功能做完了還需要工程師？

作者回顧過去開發企業軟體的經歷，當時核心任務是蒐集跨內部系統的使用者操作日誌。然而，單純抓取底層日誌並不代表交付完成，由於客戶現場經常面臨系統跳轉導致 ID 變更、遺失或跨應用呼叫，使得將操作鏈精準關聯至具體人員變得極其困難。作者指出，這類問題無法坐在辦公室透過抽象需求文檔解決，研發人員必須親赴客戶現場觀察業務人員的實際切換方式，這種模式即為矽谷著名的 FDE（Forward Deployed Engineer，前線部署工程師） 機制。

隱性知識與利益協調：現場無可取代的真實情境

作者分析，駐場的核心價值在於獲取極度稀缺的真實情境（Context）。第一線員工的日常操作大多屬於直覺習慣，是難以直接落實為文字的隱性知識；另一方面，基層員工關注操作負擔，管理層則重視合規與審批，雙方對流程往往缺乏統一認知。因此，駐場工程師承擔了兩項截然不同的任務：一是透過現場觀察補齊未記錄的實操細節，二是協助組織內部釐清分歧，共同協商並制定明確的業務規則。

產品化沉澱：交付工作的「三層架構」

為避免每個新客戶都要「從零開始」，作者團隊將現場累積的方案進行架構層面的解構，提煉出通用模組回流至核心產品，並利用外掛機制與設定檔應對個別差異。作者歸納出軟體功能完成後的「三層工作架構」：第一層是產品核心的通用處理能力（如資料蒐集與關聯）；第二層是針對特定客戶系統的外掛與適配機制；第三層則是必須由現場業務專家確認的業務語意與邊界（如正常流程與異常告警的界定）。

AI 時代的 FDE：從功能運行到真實互動與邊界測試

作者進一步指出，這套邏輯在當前大語言模型與 AI Agent 的落地中同樣適用。即使業務規則明確，系統在真實環境中仍面臨動態考驗，例如語音助理在使用者口述數字或 Email 停頓時，必須精準拿捏對話輪次（Turn-taking）而非草率介入。作者強調，無論是傳統軟體還是 AI 交付，工程評估的核心早已超越「模型或功能能否運行」，而在於能否在真實場景中嚴密應對各種複雜的邊界情況（Edge Cases）。

值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭開企業軟體交付與 AI 落地中「功能開發完成後，為何仍需工程師駐場」的核心挑戰與應對策略。
  • 深入解析 FDE（前線部署工程師） 的工作本質，說明如何挖掘未成文的「隱性知識」並調和多方業務歧異。
  • 提供清晰的「交付工作三層架構」，協助團隊有效區分核心通用模組、客製化配置以及業務邊界定義。

摘要

走進現場：為什麼功能做完了還需要工程師？

作者回顧過去開發企業軟體的經歷，當時核心任務是蒐集跨內部系統的使用者操作日誌。然而，單純抓取底層日誌並不代表交付完成，由於客戶現場經常面臨系統跳轉導致 ID 變更、遺失或跨應用呼叫，使得將操作鏈精準關聯至具體人員變得極其困難。作者指出，這類問題無法坐在辦公室透過抽象需求文檔解決，研發人員必須親赴客戶現場觀察業務人員的實際切換方式，這種模式即為矽谷著名的 FDE（Forward Deployed Engineer，前線部署工程師） 機制。

隱性知識與利益協調：現場無可取代的真實情境

作者分析，駐場的核心價值在於獲取極度稀缺的真實情境（Context）。第一線員工的日常操作大多屬於直覺習慣，是難以直接落實為文字的隱性知識；另一方面，基層員工關注操作負擔，管理層則重視合規與審批，雙方對流程往往缺乏統一認知。因此，駐場工程師承擔了兩項截然不同的任務：一是透過現場觀察補齊未記錄的實操細節，二是協助組織內部釐清分歧，共同協商並制定明確的業務規則。

產品化沉澱：交付工作的「三層架構」

為避免每個新客戶都要「從零開始」，作者團隊將現場累積的方案進行架構層面的解構，提煉出通用模組回流至核心產品，並利用外掛機制與設定檔應對個別差異。作者歸納出軟體功能完成後的「三層工作架構」：第一層是產品核心的通用處理能力（如資料蒐集與關聯）；第二層是針對特定客戶系統的外掛與適配機制；第三層則是必須由現場業務專家確認的業務語意與邊界（如正常流程與異常告警的界定）。

AI 時代的 FDE：從功能運行到真實互動與邊界測試

作者進一步指出，這套邏輯在當前大語言模型與 AI Agent 的落地中同樣適用。即使業務規則明確，系統在真實環境中仍面臨動態考驗，例如語音助理在使用者口述數字或 Email 停頓時，必須精準拿捏對話輪次（Turn-taking）而非草率介入。作者強調，無論是傳統軟體還是 AI 交付，工程評估的核心早已超越「模型或功能能否運行」，而在於能否在真實場景中嚴密應對各種複雜的邊界情況（Edge Cases）。

================================================

# 开场案例：记录采到了，却对不上人

Back when we were building software,. one of our core tasks was to collect a. person’s operation logs across. several different internal enterprise. applications. Logically speaking, once. the underlying operation logs are. captured, the task should be considered. complete, right? But in reality, it’s. far from it, because even though you. have the logs, you can’t link this. sequence of operations back to who. exactly performed them. In the. real-world scenarios of different. clients, situations vary wildly. Some. pages show account identifiers for. multiple systems; others change the. user ID the moment the system redirects. , or the ID might even go missing. entirely. Some entry points are just. the beginning. Behind the scenes,. several applications are calling each. other, so who does this continuous. chain of operations actually belong to? This isn't something we can determine. just by sitting in the office. With the. technical limitations at the time,. development and debugging had to be. done in the client's environment. We. had to watch how business users. actually switched between systems. Only. when R&D personnel went on-site and. watched them work could we decide which. information to use to accurately link. operations to individuals. When. building enterprise software, during. deployment or delivery, the features. are built and the models can provide. answers. But in a client’s real. business environment, why do we still. need engineers involved? In today’s. video, we’ll use this case study to. break down the work that remains after. the features are built. What exactly is. being solved on-site? After it’s. solved, which parts should be. integrated into the product? And which. parts must still be confirmed on-site. with every new client? Hi, hello, and.

# FDE 是什么

welcome back. This type of work has a. name: FDE, or Forward Deployed Engineer. . Actually, when we were working this. way back then, we didn't know the term.

It wasn't until later, when I read. articles written by two former Palantir. employees describing this mechanism,. that I looked back and realized our. logic was highly consistent. With the. FDE framework, we can gain much better. clarity on the work that remains after. the features are built. Why can’t.

# 为什么办公室里定不下来

this be settled in the office or. clearly written in a requirements. document? Because how frontline staff. actually operate is often the kind of. tacit, on-site knowledge that is. difficult to put directly into a. document. Industry professionals are. very familiar with their daily work. Many detailed switches and habitual. actions are taken for granted, so they. never make it into the initial. requirements list. Sitting in an office. , all you get is a highly abstract. process description that has stripped. away all the details. Only by observing. their actual operations on-site can. developers make sound engineering. judgments and fill in those unwritten. contextual details. In an article,. former PayPal engineer Neil quoted the. economist Telacon, who said that. context is what is truly scarce. He. noted that traditional enterprise. software delivery often relies solely. on a list of abstract requirements. However, in a real business environment. , what is most valuable and hardest to. obtain is precisely the real-world. context and details that cannot be. captured in documents. When we conduct. requirements analysis, we often. encounter another situation: the actual. staff and the management within the. client's organization may not share the. same understanding of processes, goals,.

or even rules. In this case, there is. no ready-made, unified answer waiting. to be discovered on-site. For example,. the operational staff cares more about. whether a certain step increases their. burden, while management focuses on. compliance and approval checkpoints. Both sides have their own set of. understandings on how to handle the. same business change. At this point,. after understanding the existing. operations on-site, engineers must also. assist the relevant parties in laying. out their respective goals, constraints. , and disagreements, clarifying them,. and helping them set the rules together. . So you see, these two types of. on-site work are completely different:. one is to observe existing practices. and uncover the tacit knowledge missing. from documents, while the other is to. help all parties clarify their. differences and negotiate unified. business rules. Both scenarios are part. of the universal complexity found in. normal business delivery. It is. precisely because of this second type. of work that you realize relying solely. on written documentation, a few rounds. of interviews, or even today’s. knowledge base retrieval is not enough. These discrepancies require engineers. to communicate and verify with the. relevant business personnel until the. rules are clear. Since every client has.

# 什么沉淀进产品，什么留在现场

a different system environment, and. their internal rules and perceptions. vary greatly, does this mean developers. must go on-site and start from scratch. every time they engage a new client? Of. course not. If every client required. starting from scratch, it would mean. that core capabilities haven't been. distilled, and there would be no talk. of true productization. We already had. a core product at the time! As more. similar clients came to us, we. proactively began to deconstruct these. on-site solutions into generalized. capabilities at the architectural level. . The account extraction,. cross-application operational. correlation, and data enrichment we. mentioned earlier were gradually. refined into standardized, universal. modules for our core product, while. handling special identifiers and. personalized redirect logic for. different client sites. We designed a. dedicated plugin mechanism and. configuration options to manage these. differences, and during this process,. it was the same group of developers who. went on-site to solve the specific. problems. Returning to the backend to. distill those common capabilities into. the core product, it was still this. very same group of developers. While. Bell described a PT organizational. structure that split engineers into.

front-line FDEs and backend core. product engineers, we had the same R&D. team take on both roles back then. Although the organizational division of. labor differed, the underlying logic. was the same: first, go to the client. site to solve the problem, then turn. the solutions useful to other clients. into product features so they could be. used in subsequent projects. But at. this point, you might ask, since the. common capabilities are already in the. product, does this mean on-site. developers are no longer needed at all? Actually, that is not the case. To give. a classic example, our general-purpose. engine could eventually parse complex. underlying technical logs directly into. business concepts that business users. could understand, but determining which. changes in these business data points. are normal processes and which. represent anomalies worth noting still. requires context from the on-site. business operations. These still. require us to work with the client's. specific business scenarios, verify the. rules one by one with on-site staff,. clarify these rules, and put the. confirmed rules into practice. Being. technically capable of parsing and. supporting data does not mean your. delivery is complete; you must work. with the business staff to define the. meaning and boundaries of these.

specific rules. After sorting these out.

# 现场工作的三层划分

and building the functionality, the. remaining on-site work is roughly. divided into three layers. The first. layer is general processing. capabilities, such as our data. collection, log parsing, cross-system. correlation, and data enrichment; these. belong to our standard capabilities. These must be integrated into our core. product, while the second layer. consists of client-specific logic—. every client has unique redirects and. system identifiers—so we must handle. those using our plugin and. configuration mechanisms. The third. layer is the specific business meaning. and boundaries—which changes are. considered normal, which metrics. require alerts, and where to draw the. lines of the business—these must be. confirmed by on-site experts who. understand the operations. Comparing. this to the previous two cases, account. association illustrates the processing. mechanism and customer adaptation,. while self-processing illustrates. business meaning and boundaries. When. we make judgments, we really look at. one thing: is the effort we are. currently spending on building usable. processing capacity and adapting to. this customer's system, or is it on. clarifying specific business rules with. the stakeholders? If you are currently. working on an enterprise software. project or an AI delivery, why not try. categorizing your project according to. these three layers? In today’s.

# AI 时代：验证系统是否按规则行动

implementation scenarios for large. models and AI agents, once the rules. are clear, you must verify if the. system actually acts according to those. rules in real-world settings. Job, who. leads the cFPDE team, gave a vivid. example in a recent company interview:. when users dictate numbers or email. addresses to a voice system, they often. pause in the middle. However, a pause. does not mean the user has finished. speaking. The voice system must be able. to judge exactly when it should take. over the conversation. Here, it is not. enough to just correctly recognize the. text; the system must also handle the. issue of dialogue turns within a real. business interaction. Job also. mentioned that during their recruitment. interviews, they provide candidates. with APIs and a knowledge base,. requiring them to build an agent within. 90 minutes. The focus of the assessment. is not just whether the agent can run,. but more importantly, how the candidate. designs tests and evaluations, and how. they handle those tricky edge cases. This engineering mechanism of going. deep into the field to solve problems. existed long before generative AI. Today’s AI has not eliminated field. work; on the contrary, because model. behavior has randomness and. interactions have latency. Combined. with current requirements for safety. and accuracy, this adds more stages. where we must conduct verification in. real-world scenarios. Furthermore,. there is a very realistic situation:. the underlying models and interfaces. are constantly changing. Once a model. is upgraded or an interface is modified. , the system behaviors that previously. complied with business rules may very. likely need to be checked all over. again. A model possessing capabilities. does not mean it can automatically. deliver results in a specific business.

# 要不要采用完整的 FDE

environment. Hearing this, it’s easy. to get the idea: since being on-site is. so critical, shouldn't all enterprise. software and AI teams simply send their. engineers to the client’s site? The vast. majority of companies actually. shouldn't adopt the full FDE model,. because in his view, a truly complete. FDE must meet three strict conditions:. first, high-value clients. The cost of. dispatching senior engineers on-site is. extremely high. Only when the contract. value is large enough can it. economically support this model. Second. , a bottom-up mindset of exploration; neither the team nor leadership should. have preset standard answers, but. rather a great passion to dive into the. front lines and grind it out with users. . Third, a platform designed for. scalability. Plus a discipline of. distinguishing what should be in the. core and what should remain at the edge. —that is, what differences stay for. client-side configuration and. development, and what commonalities. must be integrated into the core. platform. BY also provided a crucial. operational perspective: in the true. FDE logic, an engineer going to a. client site should essentially be. considered an R&D investment and a. learning opportunity, not just a. delivery cost. Because every trip to. the field is an opportunity to gather. the most authentic insights for future. general-purpose products. Comparing our.

Measuring. whether you should go down this path. isn't based on whether you send people. on-site, but on three questions: first,. are the differences between your. clients so large that they must be. solved through on-site engineering. development? question at the beginning: the features. are built, so what is still missing for. delivery? Confirm in. person; for AI delivery, you must also. verify whether the system can act. according to these rules in a. real-world scenario. Use. these practices to judge what kind of. work your project needs, distilling. tacit knowledge from the field into. general capabilities to deposit into. the product for future projects. This. was not only the underlying logic for. building enterprise software back then,. but it is also the same path I take. today for knowledge assetization.
